questions.question: What is the difference between StringBuilder and StringBuffer in Java?
questions.title: StringBuilder vs StringBuffer in Java
questions.direct_answer: Both `StringBuilder` and `StringBuffer` are mutable String alternatives — they allow in-place character modification without creating new objects on every change. The one difference: `StringBuffer` is **thread-safe** (all its methods are `synchronized`), while `StringBuilder` is **not thread-safe** but significantly faster for single-threaded code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the thread-safety distinction and can make the right choice for a given context.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always using StringBuffer 'to be safe' — its synchronisation overhead makes it slower in single-threaded code, which is 99% of the time you're building strings.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that StringBuffer exists since Java 1.0 and StringBuilder was introduced in Java 5 specifically to give a faster non-synchronized alternative. In practice, StringBuilder is almost always the right choice — if you genuinely need thread-safe string building, you usually coordinate at a higher level anyway.

sections.title: It's the Same Class Twice — One Just Carries a Lock
sections.content:
`StringBuilder` is a mutable companion to `String` — it lets you build up text in place instead of creating a new `String` each time. You make one, call `append()` as many times as you need, then call `toString()` once at the end to hand off a finished `String`.

Why does it exist at all? Because `String` is **immutable**. Every `+` or `concat()` builds a brand-new object and copies all the characters that came before. Do that inside a loop and you get **O(n²)** work — joining a thousand pieces copies the growing text a thousand times. A builder fixes this by reusing one buffer.

How does that buffer work? Internally it is a single `char[]`. `append()` writes into the next free slots. When the array fills up, it allocates a larger one — roughly **double** the size — and copies everything across once, so across many appends the total cost stays close to O(n).

Now the nuance, and the whole reason there are two classes. `StringBuffer` is exactly this design but with every method marked `synchronized`. It grabs a lock before touching the buffer, which makes it safe when **multiple threads write to the same instance**. `StringBuilder` is the identical design with the locks removed — born in **Java 5**, years after `StringBuffer` shipped in **Java 1.0**.

The gotcha: that lock is not free. In single-threaded code — which is almost all string building — it is pure overhead. That is why `StringBuilder` is the default and `StringBuffer` is the rare exception you reach for only when you can point to real concurrent writes.

sections.content:
| | `StringBuilder` | `StringBuffer` |
|---|---|---|
| Thread safe? | No | Yes — all methods synchronized |
| Performance | Faster — no lock overhead | Slower — acquires lock per method call |
| Introduced | Java 5 | Java 1.0 |
| API | Identical | Identical |
| Use when | Single-threaded (almost always) | Shared across threads (rare) |
| Preferred | Yes — default choice | Only when thread safety actually needed |

sections.title: StringBuilder in Practice — Same API as StringBuffer
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Picking `StringBuffer` "to be safe"** — its per-call lock is pure waste in single-threaded code, which is almost all string building. `StringBuilder` is the correct default, not the risky one.
- **Believing `synchronized` methods make multi-step logic thread-safe** — each *call* is atomic, but a check-then-append spanning two calls (`if (sb.length() == 0) sb.append(x)`) still races across threads. Thread safety of one method is not thread safety of your sequence.
- **Sharing a local `StringBuilder` across threads when you don't need to** — a builder created inside a method is already thread-confined; reaching for `StringBuffer` there adds lock overhead for nothing.
- **Assuming they have different APIs** — they don't. Every method matches, so switching between them is just changing the class name; there is nothing new to learn.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Identical API** — `append()`, `insert()`, `delete()`, `reverse()`, `toString()` behave the same on both; the class name is the only thing you swap.
- **`StringBuffer` is `synchronized`** — every method takes a lock, so concurrent threads can write to one instance safely, but you pay lock overhead on every call.
- **`StringBuilder` has no locks** — measurably faster in single-threaded code, which is ~99% of real string building.
- **`StringBuffer` = Java 1.0, `StringBuilder` = Java 5** — `StringBuilder` was added specifically as the unsynchronized, faster replacement.
- **`synchronized` per call ≠ atomic sequence** — even with `StringBuffer`, a check-then-act across two calls still races; genuine concurrency needs higher-level locking.
- **Default to `StringBuilder`** — only choose `StringBuffer` when you can point to multiple threads mutating the same instance.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The instinct a lot of people have is to reach for `StringBuffer` because it sounds safer — and for most code that instinct is exactly backwards. Here's the actual story. Both classes do the same job: they hold a single growable `char[]` and let you `append()` to it instead of creating a new `String` on every change. Their entire public API is identical — `append()`, `insert()`, `delete()`, `reverse()`, `toString()`.

The one real difference is synchronization. Every method on `StringBuffer` is `synchronized`, so it grabs a lock before it touches the buffer. That makes it safe when several threads write to the same instance — but it also means lock overhead on every single call, even when you're the only thread in sight.

`StringBuilder` simply drops the locks. That's the whole difference, and that's why it's faster. The history makes it click: `StringBuffer` has been around since **Java 1.0**, and by **Java 5** the team realized almost all string building happens on one thread, so they added `StringBuilder` as the unsynchronized twin.

So my rule is simple — default to `StringBuilder` every time. Only reach for `StringBuffer` if you can actually point to two threads mutating the same buffer, which in practice almost never happens, because you usually lock at a higher level anyway.

questions.question: What are the main StringBuilder methods and how do you use them?
questions.title: Main StringBuilder Methods in Java
questions.direct_answer: The most important `StringBuilder` methods are: `append(value)` to add content at the end, `insert(index, value)` to add at a position, `delete(start, end)` to remove characters, `replace(start, end, str)` to swap a range, `reverse()` to flip all characters, `charAt(i)` / `setCharAt(i, c)` to read or write a single character, and `toString()` to convert to an immutable String.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the practical StringBuilder API beyond just append() and toString(), especially for coding problems.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only knowing append() and toString() — in coding interviews StringBuilder.reverse() and deleteCharAt() come up frequently.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that append() is overloaded for all Java types (int, double, char, boolean, Object) — you never need to convert to String first. Also mention that StringBuilder has an initial default capacity of 16 characters and doubles when full.

sections.title: One Buffer, A Full Editing Toolkit
sections.content:
A `StringBuilder` is a mutable companion to `String` — it lets you build up and edit text in place instead of creating a new `String` each time. Most people meet it through `append()`, but that is just one tool on it.

Why reach past `append()`? Because real string work is not only adding to the end. You insert in the middle, cut a range out, flip the whole thing, or overwrite one character — and doing any of that with immutable `String` means slicing and re-joining, creating throwaway objects each time. A builder does it all on one buffer.

How the methods are organized makes them easy to recall. There are **adders** — `append(value)` puts content at the end, `insert(index, value)` puts it at a position. There are **removers** — `delete(start, end)` cuts a range, `deleteCharAt(index)` cuts one char. There are **editors** — `replace(start, end, str)` swaps a range, `setCharAt(index, ch)` overwrites one char, and `reverse()` flips everything. And there are **readers** — `charAt(index)`, `length()`, `indexOf(str)`, and finally `toString()`.

A nuance worth carrying: every range method follows the same rule as `substring()` — **start is inclusive, end is exclusive**. And `append()` is overloaded for every type — `int`, `double`, `char`, `boolean`, `Object` — so you never convert to `String` first.

The gotcha: every mutating method returns `this`, the *same* builder — not a new one. That is what lets you chain `sb.append(a).insert(0, b).reverse()`, but it also means there is only ever one object; the return value is not a copy.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Knowing only `append()` and `toString()`** — interview problems lean on `reverse()`, `deleteCharAt()`, and `setCharAt()`; not knowing them stalls you on otherwise simple questions.
- **Treating the end index as inclusive** — `delete(0, 3)` removes indices 0, 1, and 2 — three chars, not four. End is exclusive, exactly like `substring()`.
- **Confusing `setCharAt()` with `insert()`** — `setCharAt(i, c)` overwrites the char at `i` and keeps the length the same; `insert(i, c)` shifts everything right and grows the length by one.
- **Expecting a mutator to return a new builder** — `append()`, `reverse()`, and friends return `this`, the same object. The original is mutated in place, so there is no separate "old" copy to fall back on.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`append()` is overloaded for every type** — `int`, `double`, `char`, `boolean`, `Object` all work directly; you never call `String.valueOf()` first.
- **Range methods are start-inclusive, end-exclusive** — `delete(1, 3)` removes indices 1 and 2, not 3; the same convention as `substring()`.
- **`delete(i, i+1)` vs `deleteCharAt(i)`** — both drop one char, but `deleteCharAt` is clearer and sidesteps the off-by-one trap.
- **Every mutator returns `this`** — `append()`, `insert()`, `delete()`, `reverse()` return the same builder, so calls chain; `toString()` ends the chain.
- **`reverse()` flips in place** — the go-to for palindrome checks and string reversal in coding rounds.
- **Default capacity is 16, doubles when full** — pass a size upfront (`new StringBuilder(1000)`) for known-large strings to skip repeated array copies.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Most people stop at `append()` and `toString()`, but the methods in between are the ones that win coding rounds. I group them four ways.

To add: `append()` puts content at the end, `insert(index, value)` drops it at a position. To remove: `delete(start, end)` cuts a range, `deleteCharAt(index)` cuts one character. To edit in place: `replace(start, end, str)` swaps a range, `setCharAt(index, ch)` overwrites one char, and `reverse()` flips the whole buffer — the classic move for palindrome checks. To read: `charAt()`, `length()`, and `indexOf()`.

Two things stand out. First, `append()` is **overloaded for every Java type** — `int`, `double`, `char`, `boolean`, any `Object` — so you never convert to a `String` yourself. Second, all the range methods use the same **inclusive-start, exclusive-end** rule as `substring()`, so `delete(0, 3)` drops three characters.

One detail that shows you've actually used it: a fresh builder starts at **capacity 16 and doubles** when it fills, copying the array each time. If you know you're building something large, pass the size into the constructor and skip those copies. And since every mutator returns `this`, you chain the calls and hit `toString()` once at the end.

questions.question: When should you use String vs StringBuilder in Java?
questions.title: String vs StringBuilder — When to Use Which
questions.direct_answer: Use `String` for fixed, known values — constants, method parameters, return values, map keys, and any text that doesn't change. Use `StringBuilder` when you need to build a String piece by piece at runtime — especially in loops, conditional assembly, or when constructing large strings from many parts.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can identify the right tool for a given situation — not just knowing both exist, but knowing which scenario calls for which.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using String + in loops (O(n²)) or creating a StringBuilder for a single, simple concatenation (unnecessary verbosity).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that single-line + is fine because the compiler converts it to StringBuilder anyway. The actual performance difference only shows up in loops and conditional multi-part assembly.

sections.title: Known Text Goes in String; Text You Assemble Goes in a Builder
sections.content:
Here is the plainest version: use `String` when you already know the text, and use `StringBuilder` when you are piecing the text together at runtime. That one line answers most cases.

Why does the choice matter? Because `String` is **immutable**. Every time you change it — every `+`, every `concat()` — Java makes a new object and copies the old characters in. For a one-off join that is nothing. But put a `+` inside a loop that runs a thousand times and you have created a thousand throwaway strings, each a bit longer than the last: **O(n²)** work. `StringBuilder` keeps one growable buffer and just appends, bringing that back to roughly O(n).

So how do you actually decide? Ask whether the text is *known* or *assembled*. A constant, a method parameter, a return value, a `HashMap` key — known and complete, use `String`; it is also what every Java API expects. A value you grow in a loop, a query you build with conditional `WHERE` clauses, HTML you stitch from a template — assembled, use `StringBuilder`.

The nuance most people miss: a single-line `a + b + c` is *already* fine. The compiler quietly rewrites it into a `StringBuilder` for you, so there is nothing to optimize there. The cost only appears when the `+` sits inside a loop, because the compiler creates a brand-new builder on each iteration.

The gotcha to remember is the workbench picture. `StringBuilder` is the workbench you assemble on; `String` is the finished product you hand off. Build on the workbench, call `toString()` once, then let the workbench go — don't keep passing the builder around where a `String` belongs.

sections.title: Right Tool for Each Scenario
String vs StringBuilder — Use Case Guide
sections.content:
| Scenario | Use | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Single known value | `String` | Immutable, safe, what APIs expect |
| Single-line concatenation | `String` | Compiler converts to StringBuilder anyway |
| Loop concatenation | `StringBuilder` | Avoids O(n²) object creation |
| Conditional multi-part assembly | `StringBuilder` | One buffer, append only what's needed |
| Method parameter / return value | `String` | Java APIs expect String |
| HashMap key | `String` | Immutable — hashCode never changes |
| Thread-shared buffer | `StringBuffer` | synchronized, safe for concurrent writes |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using `+` to concatenate inside a loop** — each iteration builds a new `String` (and a new builder under the hood), turning a simple join into O(n²). Declare one `StringBuilder` before the loop and `append()` inside it.
- **Wrapping a single concatenation in a `StringBuilder`** — `new StringBuilder().append(a).append(b).toString()` for a one-liner is pure verbosity; the compiler already does exactly this for plain `a + b`.
- **Using a `StringBuilder` as a `HashMap` key** — it is mutable and uses identity `hashCode()`, so the key effectively "changes" and lookups silently fail. Keys must be `String`.
- **Returning a `StringBuilder` from a method** — hand back the finished `String` via `toString()`. Leaking the mutable buffer lets a caller corrupt your data after the fact.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`String` for known, complete text** — constants, parameters, return values, `HashMap` keys; it is immutable and what every Java API expects.
- **`StringBuilder` for runtime assembly** — loops, conditional parts, joining many fragments into one buffer.
- **Single-line `a + b + c` is already fine** — the compiler rewrites it to `StringBuilder`, so there is nothing to "optimize".
- **`+` inside a loop is the real trap** — the compiler builds a fresh `StringBuilder` each iteration, recreating the O(n²) cost; hoist one `StringBuilder` outside the loop.
- **`HashMap` keys must be `String`, not `StringBuilder`** — a builder is mutable with identity `hashCode()`, so it breaks lookups.
- **Mental model** — `StringBuilder` is the workbench, `String` is the finished product you hand off.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The cleanest way to frame it is **known versus assembled**. If you already have the text — a constant, a parameter, a return value, a map key — use `String`. It's immutable and exactly what every Java method signature is asking for. If you're building the text up at runtime, that's when `StringBuilder` earns its place.

The detail that usually separates people is what the compiler does for you. A plain `"Hello, " + name + "!"` on one line doesn't need a builder — the compiler already rewrites simple concatenation into a `StringBuilder` behind the scenes. So wrapping a single join in a manual `StringBuilder` is just noise.

Where it actually matters is **loops**. The moment a `+` sits inside a loop, the compiler creates a fresh builder on every iteration, and you're back to copying the whole growing string each time — the **O(n²)** blow-up. There you hoist one `StringBuilder` outside the loop and `append()` into it. Same story for conditional assembly, like a SQL query where you add `WHERE` clauses only when filters apply.

So my rule: don't reach for `StringBuilder` reflexively — use `String` for fixed values and single concatenations, and switch the moment you're appending in a loop or assembling conditionally. Build on it, call `toString()` once, and hand back the `String`.
